readerTitle: The $300,000 cushion that couldn't cover payroll
caseNote: 가상 사례 (금속 부품 공장, 식료품점, 소프트웨어 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 운전자본은 쌓아 둔 여유 자금이 아니라 사업을 돌리느라 고객과 재고에 묶여 있는 돈이며, 매출이 늘면 함께 늘어나 현금을 더 요구한다.
misconception: 운전자본이 클수록 재무가 튼튼하고, 이익이 나는 성장은 스스로 자금을 마련한다.

factChecks.note: 매출 50% 증가 시: 매출채권 $300,000, 재고 $225,000, 매입채무 $105,000. 현금 제외 운전자본 280,000 → 420,000, 추가로 묶이는 돈 $140,000. 현금 $20,000로는 부족하다는 계산 확인.
식료품점과 선납 캠프의 음(−) 운전자본은 일반적인 업종 특성을 설명한 것으로 특정 기업의 수치가 아닙니다. 문장에 "often"으로 일반화 수준을 낮췄습니다.
소프트웨어 사례: 연간 선불 → 분기 후불(분기 종료 60일 뒤) 전환 시 매출은 같아도 현금 수취가 늦어져 운전자본이 늘어난다는 질적 설명입니다. 구체 수치는 넣지 않았습니다.

cards.title: The $300,000 cushion that couldn't cover payroll
body: A metal parts maker gets good news from its accountant: **$300,000 in working capital**. The business looks safe.
Two weeks later, payroll is due: $40,000. The bank account holds $20,000.
Nobody made a mistake. Both numbers were true at the same time.

image.label: Factory owner holding a thick report next to a nearly empty cash box
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 공장 사무실에서 사장이 "Working capital $300,000"라고 적힌 두꺼운 보고서를 들고 있고, 책상 위 현금함은 거의 비어 있음. 뒤편에 금속 부품 상자가 쌓여 있음. 실제 로고나 상표 없음.

cards.title: A big new customer wants in.
body: You run a metal parts plant with $100,000 in monthly sales. Customers pay 60 days after delivery.
A new customer would lift your sales by 50%, at your usual margin and the same 60-day terms. Your balance sheet shows $300,000 in working capital. What's your first move?

options.text: Say yes. $300,000 in working capital covers the extra work
options.feedback: You win the order, but that $300,000 is mostly money customers owe and steel on shelves. You may not be able to buy materials or pay wages before the new customer pays.

options.text: Say yes, but first line up funding for the cash the bigger order will tie up
options.feedback: You get the growth and avoid the cash gap in the first months. It costs some planning and maybe a credit line, which is cheaper than a missed payroll.

options.text: Decline. Growing that fast is too risky
options.feedback: You protect your cash, but you give up a profitable customer. The risk is real, yet it can usually be managed rather than avoided.

cards.title: What the $300,000 was made of.
body: Most of it was money the business was *waiting* for, or steel waiting to become parts. Only $20,000 could pay a bill this week.

cards.title: Working capital
body: **Working capital** is what a business will have soon minus what it must pay soon. In accounting terms: current assets (cash, money customers owe, stock) minus current liabilities (bills due within a year, like supplier invoices).
A more useful way to see it: working capital is **money tied up in running the business** day to day. Part of it is lent to customers. Part is parked in stock.
A big number can mean safety. It can also mean a lot of cash stuck where you can't spend it.

image.label: Coins flowing out to customers and a stockroom, a few coins returning
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 가운데 금고에서 동전이 "Customers owe you"와 "Stock" 상자로 흘러가 쌓여 있고, "Suppliers" 쪽에서 동전 몇 개만 금고로 돌아옴. 금고 안에는 동전이 조금만 남아 있음.

cards.title: Grow 50%, and $140,000 more gets tied up.
body: With 50% more sales, customers owe you more and you hold more stock. Suppliers give you more credit too, but not enough to close the gap.
Before the first new customer pays, the business needs about $140,000 more in working capital. It has $20,000 in cash. Profitable growth still has to be paid for upfront.

cards.title: Some healthy businesses run below zero.
body: A grocery store often sells its milk within days but pays the dairy weeks later. A summer camp takes deposits in March for July. Customer cash arrives before the bills are due.
Here working capital can be **negative**, and that's not a warning sign. Growth brings cash in instead of tying it up.
Same measure, opposite meaning. What matters is what the number is made of, not how big it is.

cards.title: Don't shrink the number by squeezing others.
body: Paying suppliers late makes working capital look smaller. It can also cost you discounts, priority and trust. Cutting stock too far means missed orders.
Working capital is also a snapshot. A toy maker's looks very different in October than in January. Compare the same month year to year, and check what's inside the total.

cards.title: Now it's a software company.
body: Your software company bills customers a full year upfront. A large new client wants to pay quarterly, 60 days after each quarter ends.
Your sales lead says the yearly revenue is identical, so it makes no difference. What's the right read?

options.feedback: Revenue matches, but you'd go from getting cash early to waiting months after doing the work. Your working capital grows, and so does the cash you need.

options.text: Accept, but price in the later payment and plan the cash you'll carry
options.feedback: You win the client and know the cost of funding them. A higher price or a deposit can offset the cash you'll be waiting for.

options.text: Refuse any terms other than annual upfront
options.feedback: Your cash stays strong, but rigid terms can lose big deals. The terms are a cost to price, not always a reason to walk away.

cards.title: Working capital is cash at work, not cash in reserve.
body: It shows how much money your business has tied up in customers and stock. When sales grow, it usually grows too, and you fund it first.
**Try it today:** write down what customers owe you, the stock you hold and what you owe suppliers. Then ask: if sales rose 20% next month, how much more cash would get tied up?
